strengths: Well-motivated core insight: that denoising redundancy is spatially non-uniform and correlated with aesthetic-descriptor cross-attention, is intuitive and reasonably well illustrated with qualitative heatmaps (Fig. 6) and ablations (Fig. 4).

Extensive empirical evaluation: three representative DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev), a large unified protocol (10,000 Pick-a-Pic prompts, 3 seeds, 30k images per configuration), and six automatic metrics (Time, CLIP, IR, HPS, Aesthetic, Edge), which is unusually thorough for a training-free acceleration paper.

Comprehensive ablations isolating the contribution of AesMask, spatial SkipSparse, and StepCache individually and jointly (Table 7, Fig. 5), plus sensitivity studies on skip_ratio and mask_step (Tables 9-10) and token-weighting strategy comparisons (Table 8), which support the design choices.

Reasonably strong and consistent gains over multiple recent training-free baselines (Δ-DiT, FORA, TeaCache, TaylorSeer, RAS, SDiT) on speed–quality trade-off, with both quantitative tables and qualitative comparisons (Figs. 7-10).

Good transparency in the appendix regarding implementation details (anchor vocabulary, hyperparameters, hardware, backbone-specific adaptations), and an anchor-coverage analysis (Appendix E) that provides useful context on how often the method's core mechanism is actually triggered on real prompts.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim that acceleration simultaneously *improves* aesthetic/preference metrics over the dense baseline is surprising and under-analyzed; the paper attributes this to spatially-varying CFG (stronger guidance on aesthetic-focus tokens), but this conflates the effect of a guidance modification with that of computational acceleration, making it unclear how much of the reported "free lunch" comes from spatial CFG re-tuning vs genuine redundancy removal — a controlled experiment isolating spatial CFG from sparsity/caching effects on quality alone would strengthen this claim.

The core spatial SkipSparse module is architecture-dependent and does not transfer cleanly: it is disabled/altered for SD3-Medium (no spatial CFG, citing 'instability' from pilot tuning without quantitative support) and not supported in the same form for FLUX.1-dev, so two of three backbones rely mainly on the StepCache component, weakening the generality claims made in the abstract/intro about the aesthetics-driven spatial mechanism.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic/proxy metrics (ImageReward, HPS, LAION-Aesthetic, CLIP, Edge Density) with no human preference study, despite the paper's central claims being about perceptual/aesthetic quality improvements — these proxies can be gamed or biased in ways that don't reflect true human judgment.

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across backbones (e.g., RAS and SDiT are only compared on Lumina-Next, not on SD3/FLUX in Table 5/6), which limits the strength of the cross-backbone superiority claims.

Key hyperparameters (skip_ratio=0.5, mask_step=5, Δ=2) are fixed globally across all prompts/content types despite the paper's own sensitivity analysis showing non-trivial quality variation with these settings; no content-adaptive scheme is proposed, and it's unclear these defaults generalize beyond the tested prompt distribution (Pick-a-Pic, which is itself skewed toward aesthetic-heavy prompts per Appendix E).

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported despite the large evaluation set (30k images), so the magnitude of reported gains (e.g., +1-2% CLIP, few-point IR differences) cannot be assessed for robustness.
The code repository link is missing from the abstract, and while implementation details are described in the appendix, full reproducibility cannot be verified without released code.

The runtime decomposition (Table 11) shows the combined speedup is notably less than the naive sum of individual component savings, but the explanation ('mechanisms partially overlap') is only qualitative, without deeper analysis of interaction effects.

strengths: The paper is thoroughly documented: extensive appendices provide anchor vocabularies, hyperparameter tables, backbone-specific settings, hardware details, and a large battery of ablations (AesMask weighting, skip_ratio, mask_step, SkipSparse components), which aids reproducibility.

The core observation that cross-attention concentrates on tokens linked to aesthetic descriptors and that these regions evolve more over timesteps is a reasonable and intuitively motivated premise, illustrated with qualitative heatmaps (Fig. 6).

Experiments span three DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) and compare against several recent training-free acceleration baselines (RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer, FORA, Δ-DiT), and ablations isolate the contribution of spatial sparsification vs. temporal caching.
The anchor-coverage analysis (Appendix E) on Pick-a-Pic prompts is a nice sanity check showing the anchor vocabulary triggers frequently and on semantically relevant words.
weaknesses: Conflation of acceleration and quality-improvement mechanisms: the reported ImageReward/HPS/Aesthetic gains over the *dense* baseline (e.g., +11.9% IR on Lumina) plausibly stem largely from the spatially-varying CFG component (Eq. 11), which boosts guidance strength specifically on 'aesthetic' tokens—an effect essentially orthogonal to the acceleration contribution and already explored in prior work (ref. [38]). The paper never isolates spatial-CFG-only (without any sparsification/caching) to show how much of the quality gain is simply due to stronger local guidance rather than the proposed aesthetics-aware acceleration; this makes the headline 'acceleration AND quality improvement' claim difficult to trust as evidence for the stated contribution.

No human study: all 'aesthetic'/'preference' claims rest exclusively on automatic proxy metrics (ImageReward, HPS, LAION Aesthetic, CLIP, Edge density), which are known to be gameable by increased local guidance/contrast and do not reliably track human perceptual judgments. Given the paper's central thesis is about aesthetic quality, the absence of any human preference study is a significant evidentiary gap.

Limited generality of the 'full' method: the spatially-adaptive SkipSparse path (the paper's main novel acceleration mechanism) is only actually applied on Lumina-Next; on SD3-Medium spatial CFG is disabled and on FLUX.1-dev the spatial sparse path is not supported at all, so results there mostly reflect a fairly standard step-caching mechanism (comparable to TeaCache/TaylorSeer). This undercuts the claim of a unified, broadly applicable framework validated on 'three representative DiT backbones.'

Moderate novelty: the main components individually overlap substantially with prior work—region-adaptive computation budgets (RAS, SDiT), step-level caching/extrapolation (TeaCache, TaylorSeer, FORA), and spatially-varying CFG ([38]). The primary novel element is deriving the region mask from CLIP-anchor similarity to aesthetic descriptor words rather than generic saliency/semantic grouping, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

Methodological ambiguity in AesMask construction: it is unclear how per-prompt-token embeddings e(y_j) are obtained from a causal/sentence-level CLIP text encoder in a way that yields meaningful token-level similarity to isolated anchor words, and the fixed similarity threshold (0.60) and percentile mask threshold (p=0.50) are not justified beyond empirical tuning on the same evaluation set used for the main results, raising overfitting/hyperparameter-selection concerns.

No variance/statistical significance reporting despite using 3 seeds and 10,000 prompts (30,000 images); all tables report single point estimates, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (e.g., 0.841 vs 0.822 IR in ablations) are meaningful or within noise.

The claim of spatio-temporal non-uniformity being 'coupled' (aesthetic regions vary more over time) is asserted qualitatively but not quantitatively validated (e.g., no correlation statistic between attention concentration and temporal variance of predictions is reported).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core insight: coupling aesthetic-descriptor-driven cross-attention concentration with spatio-temporal redundancy for training-free DiT acceleration is a fresh angle relative to prior uniform token-merging/caching methods.

Extensive empirical validation across three distinct DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) and against six strong training-free baselines (Δ-DiT, FORA, RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer), evaluated on a large, fixed 10k-prompt/3-seed protocol for fair, paired comparison.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of AesMask vs. SkipSparse spatial path vs. StepCache temporal path, plus sensitivity analyses on skip_ratio and mask_step with both quantitative tables and qualitative figures.

Useful supplementary analyses (Appendix E) quantifying anchor trigger rates and most frequent matched anchors on real Pick-a-Pic prompts, which helps ground the method's practical applicability and clarifies fallback behavior when no anchors are triggered.

Reports a rare simultaneous improvement in both speed and preference-oriented quality metrics (ImageReward, HPS, Aesthetic score) rather than the typical speed-quality trade-off, supported by consistent qualitative examples.
Reasonably detailed implementation and reproducibility information (anchor vocabulary, hyperparameter tables, hardware/precision settings) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core spatial contribution (AesMask + SkipSparse spatial sparsification) is only fully realized on Lumina-Next; on SD3 and FLUX the reported gains are attributed mainly to the StepCache temporal path (spatial CFG disabled on SD3, spatial SkipSparse unsupported on FLUX), which somewhat undercuts the claimed generality of the paper's central novel idea across DiT architectures.

All quality claims rely exclusively on automated preference/aesthetic proxies (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic, CLIP, Edge Density) without any human study; since these reward models are known to be imperfect and exploitable, the counter-intuitive finding that reduced compute *improves* ImageReward over the dense baseline warrants stronger validation (e.g., human preference study or at least discussion of why/whether this reflects a real perceptual gain vs. reward-model artifact).
No standard fidelity metric such as FID/KID is reported, leaving open whether the reallocation strategy affects overall distributional image quality besides preference-model scores.

Results are reported as point estimates over 30,000 images without variance or confidence intervals, making it hard to judge the statistical significance of sometimes small margins (e.g., HPS differences in the third decimal place).

The anchor-based aesthetic-token selection relies on a fixed, English, manually curated 34-word vocabulary and CLIP similarity threshold; its robustness to different languages, domains, or prompts with implicit (non-lexical) aesthetic cues is not evaluated, and fallback behavior (uniform weighting) reduces the method to existing baselines in a meaningful fraction of cases.

Some conceptual overlap with existing region-adaptive methods (RAS, SDiT) is acknowledged but the empirical gap in reported baseline numbers (e.g., SDiT underperforming markedly) raises a question of whether baseline reproduction was fully optimized, which is important for a fair comparison given the paper's central claim of superiority in region-adaptive design.

Experiments are conducted on a single GPU/batch size configuration; scaling behavior (larger batch sizes, different resolutions, other samplers) is not explored, which limits confidence in generality of the reported speedups.

strengths: Well-motivated core idea: coupling aesthetics-driven spatial non-uniformity (via cross-attention to a curated aesthetic-anchor vocabulary) with temporal prediction redundancy is a reasonably fresh angle relative to purely saliency-agnostic caching/pruning methods.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) and against six representative training-free acceleration baselines (Δ-DiT, FORA, RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer), evaluated on a large, fixed 10k-prompt/3-seed protocol for fair, paired comparisons.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of AesMask vs. SkipSparse (spatial) vs. StepCache (temporal), plus sensitivity studies on skip_ratio and mask_step, and a runtime decomposition table, which help clarify which component drives which gain.

Includes a blind human preference study, prompt/scene robustness checks (descriptor-free prompts, six hard-scene categories), a distilled-model (FLUX.1-schnell) compatibility check, and an anchor-vocabulary coverage analysis, going beyond automatic metrics alone to substantiate claims.

Reasonably clear technical exposition with formal notation for the mask construction, sparse attention/FFN update rule, spatial CFG, and step-level linear extrapolation caching, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of simultaneously accelerating inference AND improving aesthetic/preference metrics across nearly every backbone and metric is a strong 'free lunch' claim that is not fully disentangled: a substantial part of the quality gain appears attributable to the spatially varying CFG (stronger guidance on aesthetic-focus tokens), which is a generation-altering intervention rather than a pure acceleration technique, making comparisons with baselines that do not modify guidance somewhat confounded. The paper does report gains on SD3 where spatial CFG is disabled, but does not clearly explain the mechanism producing quality improvement there.

All evaluation relies on learned preference/aesthetic scoring functions (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION-Aesthetic, CLIP, Edge density) that are known to be susceptible to reward-hacking effects such as increased sharpness/contrast from stronger effective guidance; no FID, precision/recall, or other distribution-level fidelity/diversity metric is reported to rule out such artifacts.

The technical novelty is incremental: the acceleration mechanisms (region-adaptive sparse attention with global KV, FFN caching, step-level linear extrapolation) are combinations/adaptations of existing ideas (RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer-style caching); the main novel element is the CLIP-anchor-word-based semantic prior for mask construction, which is a relatively simple, hand-crafted heuristic (34 fixed anchor words) whose generality to prompts without explicit aesthetic descriptors or non-English/other-domain prompts is not deeply examined.

Anchor coverage analysis shows only ~45% of a broad prompt pool trigger a strong anchor hit (vs. 65% on the curated evaluation subset), raising concern about how the top-r fallback selection behaves and whether reported gains generalize to more typical, non-aesthetic-adjective-laden prompts encountered in deployment.

Main results (Table 1) and most ablations report single point estimates without variance/confidence intervals despite averaging over thousands of images, limiting assessment of statistical robustness of the reported deltas.

The human study is relatively small (15 annotators, 60 pairs) with limited detail on annotator expertise/agreement, and the unified PyTorch-only implementation (no FlashAttention/kernel-level optimization) may not reflect real deployment speedups, which is acknowledged but still limits practical impact claims.

The manuscript's appendix explicitly frames a large fraction of the supplementary evidence as 'Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments,' which is unusual for an initial submission and suggests the presented evidence was reactively assembled rather than part of an originally coherent evaluation design; this does not itself invalidate the results but raises questions about selection effects in what is reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem (training-free DiT acceleration) and attempts to connect efficiency gains with perceptual/aesthetic quality rather than treating acceleration as a purely numerical-fidelity trade-off.

The experimental protocol is fairly extensive: three DiT backbones, a large prompt set (10k Pick-a-Pic prompts, 3 seeds), six automatic metrics, and a blind human preference study (15 annotators x 60 pairs) that partially corroborates the automatic-metric gains.

The ablation studies (AesMask token-weighting, SkipSparse components, skip_ratio and mask_step sensitivity, runtime decomposition) are thorough and help clarify the individual contribution of each proposed component.
The method is training-free and architecture-agnostic in spirit, requiring no retraining or fine-tuning, which is attractive for practical deployment.
The writing and mathematical formalization of the AesMask and SkipSparse mechanisms are mostly clear and the figures (heatmaps, mask overlays, radar charts) aid understanding of the core idea.
weaknesses: The central claimed contribution—jointly applying AesMask-guided spatial sparsity, Spatial-CFG, and StepCache—is in fact only realized in full on one of the three backbones (Lumina-Next). On SD3 spatial CFG is disabled, and on FLUX the spatial SkipSparse path is not used at all, leaving only generic step-caching (a well-established technique). This substantially weakens the paper's central claim of a generalizable 'aesthetics-aware spatio-temporal' acceleration framework, since two of three backbones do not actually exercise the paper's main novel mechanism.

The core idea of allocating compute non-uniformly to semantically/attention-salient regions is not new (e.g., RAS, SDiT, and other region-adaptive or saliency-based sparsification methods are cited as closely related). The specific novelty here—using a hand-picked list of 34 'aesthetic' anchor words and CLIP similarity to define salient tokens—is a fairly narrow and somewhat ad hoc heuristic rather than a principled or broadly justified mechanism; it is unclear this differs meaningfully from generic prompt-salience-driven masking already explored by prior region-adaptive methods.

On FLUX.1-dev, the one setting with full automatic-metric comparisons, AccelAes achieves a lower speedup (1.73x) than TeaCache (2.14x) or TaylorSeer (2.12x) while only marginally improving ImageReward (1.317 vs 1.304) and CLIP, undermining the paper's central 'better speed-quality trade-off' narrative in the one case most representative of modern commercial-scale DiTs.

Evaluation relies heavily on automatic preference/aesthetic metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic, CLIP) that are themselves learned reward/scoring models; because AesMask construction and quality evaluation both hinge on semantically/aesthetically-charged textual or visual cues, there is a risk of favorable correlation/metric-gaming rather than demonstrated genuine perceptual improvement. The human study, while a nice addition, is modest in scale (60 pairs) and does not fully resolve this concern, especially since alignment win-rate vs. the dense baseline is the one comparison that does not reach significance.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the large-scale (10k-prompt, 30k-image) automatic-metric results, so it is difficult to judge whether reported differences (e.g., CLIP 0.2531 vs 0.2640) are statistically meaningful or within measurement noise.

The supplementary material contains an explicit 'Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments' appendix framed as responses to prior reviewer concerns, which is unusual and concerning for an initial submission—this suggests the manuscript may be a resubmission with leftover rebuttal framing not properly reintegrated, raising questions about the preparation and anonymization quality of the submitted version.

The anchor-word vocabulary is manually curated and English/style-adjective-specific, raising generalizability concerns for prompts in other languages, styles, or domains (e.g., technical/scientific imagery) where 'aesthetic' descriptors are absent or different; the paper's descriptor-free experiment only partially addresses this.

No code link is provided (placeholder left blank) and several implementation details (e.g., which cross-attention layers are aggregated, exact percentile computation per architecture) are deferred to the appendix, which combined with the missing repository raises reproducibility concerns.

Comparisons omit some more recent/strong baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., SpargeAttention, MosaicDiff, OmniCache), limiting the completeness of the empirical positioning against the current state of the art.

strengths: The core motivation—that aesthetic-oriented prompt tokens induce spatially concentrated cross-attention and that this signal can jointly guide both acceleration and quality preservation—is an interesting and relatively underexplored angle compared to purely numerical-similarity-based caching/pruning methods.

The experimental protocol is unusually thorough for a training-free acceleration paper: three DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev), a fixed 10k-prompt/3-seed evaluation set, six automatic metrics, a blind human preference study (15 annotators x 60 pairs x 4 questions with statistical testing), and an extensive appendix with ablations on skip_ratio, mask_step, token-weighting strategies, runtime decomposition, anchor-coverage analysis, complex-scene/descriptor-free robustness, distilled-model compatibility, and failure-case mitigation.

The ablation studies (Fig. 5, Tables 8-11) cleanly separate the contributions of AesMask, spatial SkipSparse, and StepCache, showing each module's speed/quality trade-off individually and in combination, which supports the claimed complementarity.

The method is training-free and largely architecture-agnostic in its temporal-caching component, with reasonable adaptation notes explaining why spatial SkipSparse and spatial-CFG are disabled for certain backbones (SD3, FLUX).

Qualitative results and attention visualizations (Figs. 6-7) provide intuitive support for the claim that aesthetic-relevant regions receive concentrated attention and benefit from preserved computation.
weaknesses: The headline claim that acceleration simultaneously improves perceptual quality over the dense baseline is not fully disentangled from the effect of Spatial-CFG, which explicitly raises the guidance scale on masked/aesthetic-relevant tokens (Eq. 11). Since increasing CFG scale is a well-known way to boost ImageReward/HPS/Aesthetic-score metrics (which are known to be gameable via guidance strength), part of the reported quality gain could stem from an effectively higher/region-biased guidance scale rather than from the acceleration mechanism itself. The human study shows a 66% win rate even for "AccelAes vs. w/o Spatial-CFG," underscoring that guidance modulation is a major driver of the quality gain, which somewhat blurs the paper's framing of "acceleration that also improves quality."

There is no baseline comparing a dense model with an equivalently raised (but spatially uniform) global CFG scale to check whether the spatial redistribution of guidance is actually necessary, or whether similar IR/HPS gains could be obtained simply by increasing the global guidance scale without any masking or acceleration. This weakens the causal claim that aesthetics-aware spatial allocation—rather than guidance-scale tuning—is responsible for the improvements.

The core spatially-adaptive SkipSparse mechanism (the paper's central technical novelty) is only fully demonstrated on one of the three backbones (Lumina-Next); for SD3-Medium spatial CFG is disabled, and for FLUX.1-dev the spatial path is not used at all, with the reported gains there coming mainly from StepCache (a fairly standard caching idea). This limits the generality of the paper's central contribution despite the abstract's claim of consistent behavior "across representative DiT families."

Per-backbone hyperparameter and module configuration differs substantially (spatial CFG on/off, different skip ratios implied), suggesting the method requires non-trivial per-architecture tuning rather than being a single unified training-free recipe, which is somewhat at odds with the "universal" framing of StepCache and the general framework claims.

The human preference study, while a valuable addition, is relatively small in scale (60 pairs, 15 annotators) for validating quality claims across three backbones and multiple ablation variants; only one pairwise comparison set is reported, and it's unclear whether it covers all backbones or is Lumina-specific.

The anchor-based CLIP-similarity approach for identifying aesthetic tokens relies on a fixed, manually curated 34-word English vocabulary; robustness to different languages, unusual aesthetic vocabulary, or prompts that do not match the anchor list beyond the diagnostic coverage analysis is not deeply investigated (44.9%/65.5% coverage figures suggest a large fraction of prompts have weak or no strong anchor matches, and behavior in this regime is only lightly addressed).
